St. Mary’s Commissioners Approve New Permit Process For Charitable Gaming Devices

Free county permits will help distinguish authorized machines operated by nonprofit and fraternal organizations from unregulated gaming devices.
by Sophia Blackwell September 17, 2026September 16, 2026

Share this:

  • Link copied
  • Share on X (Opens in new window) X
  • Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook
  • Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:42
Instaread

LEONARDTOWN, Md. — Charitable and fraternal organizations operating certain games of chance in St. Mary’s County will now need a county permit under regulations unanimously approved by the Commissioners of St. Mary’s County on Sept. 15.

The commissioners adopted a resolution designating the St. Mary’s County Attorney’s Office to administer the new permit program. County Attorney Buffy Giddens and Deputy County Attorney John Sterling Houser presented the proposal, which was developed in response to a new state law that took effect July 1.

“This was designed to be a very simple process at the local level — kind of keep doing business as you’ve been doing, because nothing is now legal or illegal that wasn’t previously,” Houser told the commissioners. “The only change going forward is that a permit from the county is going to be required.”

The permits will be free.

The change stems from House Bill 610, which became Chapter 555 of the 2026 Laws of Maryland. The law requires qualified organizations to obtain a permit when operating covered gaming devices in St. Mary’s County and directs the commissioners to designate someone to administer the process.

Under the law, qualified organizations include volunteer fire companies and bona fide religious, fraternal, civic, veterans and charitable organizations.

Covered gaming devices include mechanisms used to play games of chance, such as paddle wheels, wheels of fortune, chance books, Nevada cards and stamp machines. Slot machines are expressly excluded.

Raffles, carnivals and bazaars also remain exempt from the county permit requirement. Bingo will continue to be governed under the county’s existing licensing regulations.

“For the record, for now and forever, raffles, carnivals and bazaars are exempt from the county permitting requirement unless the law changes,” Houser said. “You do not need to come in and get a county permit for your church raffle, your Queen of Hearts draw, nothing else.”

Houser said the new rules are intended primarily for gaming machines that remain at an organization’s location throughout the year.

Hewitt Questions State And Local Oversight

Commissioner Mike Hewitt questioned how the county permits would interact with the authority of the Maryland State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission.

Hewitt said local lodges previously faced decisions about whether to continue offering certain gaming machines or lottery products. He asked what organizations should watch for under the new system and whether inspections would be conducted by the county, law enforcement or state regulators.

Houser explained that St. Mary’s County previously did not have a local permitting requirement for the covered devices. That made it difficult for state regulators to determine whether machines they encountered were authorized under the county’s local gaming laws.

The new permit system will create a county record showing which qualified organizations operate the devices and where those machines are located.

“There are no plans to do that level of enforcement at the local level,” Houser said when asked about spot inspections.

Instead, county oversight is expected to occur primarily through applications, annual reports and complaints. The resolution does not establish a separate inspection unit or active enforcement program.

Organizations will be required to report each machine’s income, expenses and remaining proceeds annually. They must also certify that the money was used for purposes allowed under state law and that no individual member or guest profited from the machines.

“I don’t think that’s going to be an issue for anybody, because these are all used for charitable purposes anyway,” Hewitt said.

State Retains Final Authority

While the county will issue the permits, Houser emphasized that the Maryland State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission retains final authority over whether a particular machine is legal or suitable for operation.

If state regulators make a determination about a machine, that decision would supersede the county’s local regulations.

Houser also cautioned organizations against assuming that a machine permitted elsewhere in Maryland is automatically allowed in St. Mary’s County.

“Do not, because you see it in another county in Maryland, assume that it can be done the same way here,” he said. “Each county has different local rules.”

How The Permit Process Will Work

Giddens said the County Attorney’s Office anticipates creating a web-based application that qualified organizations can submit online. Organizations will also be able to visit the County Attorney’s Office in the Chesapeake Building in Leonardtown to complete the process.

One permit will cover all gaming devices an organization intends to operate during the year. Each device must be disclosed and will be tracked individually using its serial number and a county-issued identification number.

State law limits an organization to operating no more than five covered gaming devices in a building or on the same day. An organization may own additional devices and rotate them, but each machine must be listed with the county.

Applicants will also need to demonstrate that they are bona fide qualified organizations. The county may request articles of incorporation, an IRS Form 990 or another filing showing the organization’s charitable or tax-exempt status. Applicants will also need to provide a certificate of good standing and proof that they are authorized to operate in Maryland.

The County Attorney’s Office will maintain permit records, provide identification information for approved devices, remind organizations about reporting requirements and review annual reports. Permits may be renewed, suspended, revoked or denied renewal based on compliance.

The resolution may be amended later if county officials determine that additional regulations or enforcement measures are needed.

Organizations seeking information about the new gaming-device permits may contact the St. Mary’s County Attorney’s Office at 301-475-4200, ext. 1700, or ctyatt@stmaryscountymd.gov. The office is located in the Chesapeake Building at 41770 Baldridge St. in Leonardtown.
